Parish Politics

By PETER STEINFELS

 After World War II, Roman Catholicism and the American image converged

AMERICAN CATHOLIC

 The Saints and Sinners Who Built America's Most Powerful Church.

 By Charles R. Morris.
 Illustrated. 511 pp. New York:
 Times Books/Random House. $27.50.

CATHOLIC CONVERTS

 British and American Intellectuals Turn to Rome.

 By Patrick Allitt.
 343 pp. Ithaca, N.Y.:
 Cornell University Press. $35.

 THE SMOKE OF SATAN

 Conservative and Traditionalist Dissent in Contemporary American Catholicism.

 By Michael W. Cuneo.
 214 pp. New York:
 Oxford University Press. $27.50.

 
etween the mid-1940's and the mid-50's, something very strange took place in American religious and cultural history. A century earlier, anti-Catholic
                    mobs in half a dozen American cities had burned convents, churches and Irish neighborhoods. Armed Irishmen, when they weren't standing guard around their parish buildings, fought pitched retaliatory battles with nativists. In
                    the decade when World War II flowed into the cold war, however, Catholicism became the very face of postwar ''Americanism.''
                

                    In three consecutive years, 1943, 1944 and 1945, movies centering on Roman Catholicism -- ''Song of Bernadette,'' ''Going My Way,'' ''The Bells of St. Mary's'' and ''The Keys of
                    the Kingdom'' -- were nominated for 34 Oscars and won 12. The Catholic priest, once a sinister figure in the American imagination, actually became a cinematic model of American manhood. From Spencer Tracy's Father Flanagan
                    in ''Boys' Town''; Bing Crosby's crooning ex-baseball player, Father Chuck O'Malley; Karl Malden's labor priest in ''On the Waterfront''; and assorted roles by Pat O'Brien,
                    there emerged the ''superpadre'': virile, wise, good-humored, compassionate and, in emergencies, possessed of a remarkable knockout punch. So what if they were celibate? So (apparently) was the Lone Ranger.
                

                    In those years, the Catholic Church was to morality and uplift what General Motors was to industry and the Yankees were to baseball. On television the inspiring lectures of Bishop Fulton J. Sheen, with a peak audience of 30 million, swamped the Tuesday
                    night competition, Milton Berle's comedy hour, to become the nation's most popular television program.
                

                    Rendering this convergence between Catholicism and the American image all the more paradoxical was that its roots were in what Charles R. Morris in ''American Catholic'' calls the church's ''prickly apartness.''
                    Beginning in the middle of the 19th century, the controlling faction within the American Catholic hierarchy created what Morris occasionally calls a ''state-within-a-state''; it could more accurately be called a
                    culture within a culture -- an all-enveloping cocoon of institutions, beliefs and practices that was ''in America, usually enthusiastically for America, but never quite of America.''
                

                    The template for this American-but-not-quite-American church was a rigorous Catholicism forged in famine-shattered Ireland and reinforced by the generally embattled posture of the 19th-century papacy. The Irish-born prelates who dominated the American
                    hierarchy shrewdly adapted it to American conditions and imposed its discipline on other immigrant groups, some of whom arrived enjoying more relaxed versions of the faith.
                

                    The key invention here was a parochial school system that had no parallel elsewhere in the world. But the schools did not stand alone. For all the rhythms of the calendar, phases in life and crises of body and soul, the church offered devotions, services,
                    organizations and authoritative counsel. In fact, only in the mid-60's did as many as half the Catholic children of school age attend Catholic schools, a cresting of the wave well after the distinctive Catholic culture had begun
                    to come apart, undermined by its own success in equipping Catholics to enter the American mainstream.
                

                    The last third of Morris's book describes the ''crisis'' that has ensued as the church gropes for a new vision to replace its earlier semi-separatism. It is a picture drawn with the fresh eyes of someone clearly not enlisted in
                    any of the rigid camps that unfortunately divide contemporary Catholic leadership. But this picture is more familiar to most people than the history Morris recounts with such verve in earlier chapters.
                

                    He delivers this history in vivid accounts of events and personalities, whether the 1834 mob burning of the Ursuline Convent in Charlestown, Mass., the ghastly consequences of potato blight in rural Ireland or the cutthroat maneuverings of rival archbishops
                    for favor in Rome.
                

                    Woven into the opening chapter's rich description of the laying of the cornerstone for St. Patrick's Cathedral in New York in 1858 and the cathedral's dedication in 1879 is a whole panorama of the church's brash attempt to shoulder
                    its way into the resistant ranks of the urban establishment.
                

                    Likewise, Morris captures the contradictory strengths and impulses of separatist Catholicism at its high-water mark in an original chapter on Dennis Cardinal Dougherty of Philadelphia, a man who liked to style himself ''God's bricklayer''
                    for all the parish schools and churches constructed (usually in that order) during his tenure from 1918 to 1951. In 1934, the autocratic Dougherty expressed his displeasure with Hollywood by simply forbidding all Philadelphia Catholics,
                    on pain of serious sin, to attend any movies at all. The threat by 525 Philadelphia-area theater operators to close down and throw thousands of Catholics out of work in mid-Depression did not move him. Neither did the inconsistency
                    of his total ban with his fellow bishops' efforts to develop the Legion of Decency's rating system for movies. Dougherty renewed his ban in 1935 and never rescinded it. In theory, Morris slyly suggests, Philadelphia Catholics
                    are still committing a grievous sin every time they go to the movies.
                

                    Dougherty was intelligent (he spoke 10 languages, at least five of them fluently), brilliant at real estate and cruelly insensitive toward his priests. He was complacent about his flock's racism and unembarrassed about the contrast between his grand
                    style of living and the privations of the working-class Catholics who supported it. Yet he also included Jews among his closest friends, he forced the Vatican to open new opportunities for nuns, he defied the rest of the hierarchy
                    in endorsing an equal rights amendment for women in the 40's and he cultivated in private a deep mystical streak.
                

                    Morris -- who has written books on subjects as diverse as New York City politics and the computer industry -- does not evade sensitive topics, from Irish Catholic attitudes toward African-Americans at the time of the Civil War to the Vatican's dealings
                    with fascist regimes in the 20th century. In almost every case, his judgments are both nuanced and unapologetic. Furthermore, reading his firsthand reporting on the contemporary church was at times eerie: he and I happen to have visited
                    some of the same parishes across the country and even, it seems, attended the same sessions at one gathering of theologians. In every case, I can vouch for the accuracy of his observations.
                

                    Until World War II, in both England and the United States, converts supplied the church's intellectual leadership. They were much better prepared educationally than the working-class immigrants who constituted the bulk of the faithful, and they were
                    conversant with the surrounding non-Catholic culture.
                

                    In ''Catholic Converts,'' Patrick Allitt, an associate professor of history at Emory University, ushers a fascinating cast of these converts on and off his stage: major figures like John Henry Newman, Orestes Brownson, G. K. Chesterton,
                    Graham Greene, Evelyn Waugh, Dorothy Day, Thomas Merton and Marshall McLuhan, but also less well-known figures like Richard Simpson, a tireless critic of the temporal and spiritual claims made by the 19th-century papacy, and St. George
                    Mivart, an expert in primate anatomy who criticized Darwin but argued his own form of evolution and was eventually excommunicated for his then-maverick views on everything from hell to church history.
                

                    UNDOUBTEDLY, such figures were important in the church's intellectual life. Just how important intellectual life was in the progress of the church, at least in the United States, is another matter. Very few of these names turn up in Morris's
                    account.
                

                    That is also true of the wilder tribes of American Catholic conservatism reported on by Michael W. Cuneo in ''The Smoke of Satan.'' Here are feverish critics who regard the Catholic bishops as milquetoasts on sexual ethics and abortion.
                    Here are poor souls whose distress over changes in traditional doctrine or liturgy has flowered into true night gardens of conspiracy theory. Some believe that the Second Vatican Council was a plot of Communists and Freemasons, and
                    therefore the Popes who endorsed the council's work must have been either satanic anti-Popes or impostors placed on the throne of Peter by mysterious forces that had kidnapped and imprisoned the genuine Pontiffs. Others find the
                    key to history in secret instructions from the Blessed Virgin, often to themselves, and denounce church leaders who refuse to march to these orders.
                

                    This colorful fringe, Cuneo makes clear, does not weigh heavily on the church's organizational life. Nor does it represent anything parallel to the Protestant religious right. Lack of influence doesn't make these people uninteresting, of course,
                    and sometimes they're even poignant, in their determination to live out convictions that tie them into theological knots and put them at odds with the very church whose teaching they claim to follow without deviation. Cuneo, who
                    teaches sociology and anthropology at Fordham University, is a sympathetic reporter, to the point of occasionally seeming to share his subjects' utterly bleak view of the contemporary church. But he also reports nuttiness as nuttiness.
                

                    There is indeed a significant conservative revival in American Catholicism, one outfitted with ideas, energy, money, considerable support from leading bishops and open lines to the Vatican. A few actors in this revival are mentioned in Cuneo's pages;
                    most are not. But it would be a mistake and a distortion to confuse them with the genuine wackos who occupy most of his attention.
                

                    ''Catholic Converts'' provides an interesting sidelight to Morris's history, and ''The Smoke of Satan'' exhibits a regular sideshow to the contemporary scene. But to anyone looking for a single book to unfold
                    the rich, paradoxical religious reality of over 60 million Americans, I heartily recommend ''American Catholic.''
                

Peter Steinfels, who writes the Beliefs column for The New York Times, is a visiting professor of history at Georgetown University.
